Now consider several other approaches investors sometimes use to decide which stocks to buy. For each approach below, please indicate whether you have heard of it before.

  • Fundamental Strength: Buying companies with strong financial health, such as high profits or solid finances.

  • Price Momentum: Buying stocks whose prices have been rising, expecting the trend to continue.

  • Peer Influence: Buying stocks recommended or owned by trusted people, such as friends or family.
  • Valuation (Undervalued Stocks): Buying stocks that look cheap compared to what one thinks they are really worth.
  • Buying the Dip: Buying after a price drop believed to be temporary.
  • ESG/Personal-values-based Investing: Buying companies that match one’s ethical, social, or environmental values.
  • Technical Analysis: Buying based on technical indicators or chart patterns.
  • None of the above

parts.note_text: This figure shows how effective the follow-up survey respondents believe each of the thirteen heuristics to be. On a five-point scale from 1 (“not effective at all”) to 5 (“extremely effective”), respondents rate how effective a heuristic is at finding stocks that match an investment objective in their own local stock market. The rated heuristics are those we identify in the interview of the respondent plus any others the respondent reports having used in the past. When these exceed three, the respondent rates only the three longest-used. We elicit ratings only for the objectives the respondent rates 4 or 5 in importance, so every rating comes from a respondent who has used the heuristic and considers the objective important. Twenty-one respondents rate no objective that highly and therefore rate no heuristic. The figure pools the four objectives. Because a respondent rates between one and four objectives, we first average the ratings of each respondent for a heuristic across the objectives she rates and then average across respondents, so that each respondent counts equally. Markers report these means and horizontal bars the associated 95% confidence intervals, and we truncate the horizontal axis to the range of the estimates. This table examines whether investors adopt the heuristics they perceive as effective for the objectives they consider important, re-estimating the linear probability models of Table 6 of the main paper as fixed-effects logit models. The logit estimation drops fixed-effect groups without variation in the outcome, because the group effect fits their observations perfectly, which leaves 3,291, 3,291, and 3,181 observations in Columns (1) through (3), respectively. Coefficients are in log-odds and are therefore not directly comparable in scale to the linear probability estimates. The row Pseudo R² reports McFadden’s pseudo-R², computed against an intercept-only logit on the estimation sample of each column. parts.note_text: This table repeats the analysis of Table 8 of the main paper over post-adoption periods based on reported use durations. For each adopted heuristic, we use the duration of current use or, if the investor has stopped using it, the duration before stopping. We exclude investor–heuristic pairs that report a few months or an unknown duration. Taking June 30, 2026 as the common reference date, we use minimum durations of one and three years for reports of one to three years and more than three years, respectively. Monthly portfolio sorts therefore begin in July 2025 or July 2023, and we measure delivery over the month following each sort. Outcomes cover August through December 2025 (five months) or August 2023 through December 2025 (29 months, the longest period). The average period is approximately 20 months per investor, with retained heuristics weighted equally within each investor. We evaluate the choices recorded in the interviews through December 2025, including heuristics no longer used. For returns, we calculate the CAPM alpha with market betas fixed at their heuristic–country estimates from July 2013 through June 2023 portfolio sorts. For upside and stability, we use the top-1% hit-rate spread and the sign-reversed total return volatility spread. We standardize outcomes in both periods using the within-objective means and sample standard deviations across the seventy heuristic–country pairs in the 29-month window. Prioritized objectives and aggregation are otherwise as in Table 8 of the main paper. The two benchmark rows replace the retained adopted set of each investor with an equally sized random draw without replacement from (i) the covered heuristics she did not adopt in the interview (Alternative heuristics) and (ii) all seven covered heuristics (Randomly selected heuristics). The first pool also excludes adopted heuristics dropped by the duration filter. We randomly assign the drawn heuristics to the periods of the adopted heuristics and evaluate them in the same country on the same prioritized objectives. These two rows report means across 10,000 draws, with standard deviations across draws in parentheses, and their p-values are the one-sided fraction of draws that deliver at least as much as the adopted set. The sample comprises 371 investors and 621 retained investor–heuristic pairs. The columns Returns, Upside, and Stability use 180, 137, and 224 of these investors, respectively. Interpreting these results as post-adoption delivery assumes that the reported durations identify the start of use and that the reported priorities apply during the evaluation period. Statistical significance at the 10%, 5%, and 1% levels is denoted by *, **, and ***, respectively, referring to the p-values in the brackets.
